title: Noodle RAT Uses Scheduled Tasks, Cron Jobs and Process Spoofing to Hide on Systems
content_md: Noodle RAT, also tracked as ANGRYREBEL and Nood RAT, is a modular remote access trojan used by Chinese-speaking threat actors to maintain covert access to Windows and Linux systems. Active since at least mid-2016, the malware was once incorrectly identified as a Gh0st RAT or Rekoobe variant. Researchers now classify it as a distinct backdoor family with separate Windows and Linux builds. The malware is designed for long-term access, data theft, and network movement. Its operators use scheduled tasks, cron jobs, startup mechanisms, encrypted communications, and process spoofing to remain hidden after an initial compromise. Noodle RAT has appeared in espionage and financially motivated campaigns across the Asia-Pacific region, including targets in Thailand, India, Japan, Malaysia, and Taiwan. Threat groups associated with its use include Iron Tiger, Calypso APT, Rocke, and Cloud Snooper. The broad range of operators suggests that the malware is flexible enough for both suspected state-linked espionage and cybercrime operations. Noodle RAT Hides Persistently The Windows version, known as Win.NOODLERAT, is an in-memory modular backdoor. Attackers can load it through shellcode using loaders such as MULTIDROP and MICROLOAD, reducing the need to store a full malware executable on disk. Once active, the Windows implant can upload and download files, run additional modules, create a TCP proxy, execute commands, and delete itself.
